label: The Arithmetic of Knots
notes: Open the lecture. Knots can be added, and this addition behaves remarkably like multiplication of integers. The lecture follows printed pages 21 through 28 and develops the connected sum operation, the notion of prime knots, the unique factorization theorem for knots, and the role of the unknot as a multiplicative identity.

label: Connected Sum
notes: Define the connected sum of two knots: cut each open and splice the loose ends together to form a single knot. With care about orientation this operation is well defined, commutative, and associative. It is the basic way to build complicated knots from simpler ones and the analogue of multiplying numbers.

label: The Unknot as Identity
notes: Observe that adding the unknot to any knot leaves it unchanged, so the unknot is the identity for connected sum. Crucially there are no inverses: you can never untie a nontrivial knot by adding another knot. This irreversibility, proved using genus, is what makes the arithmetic interesting and rigid.

label: Prime Knots
notes: Call a nontrivial knot prime when it cannot be written as a connected sum of two nontrivial knots. The trefoil and figure-eight are prime, and prime knots are the indivisible building blocks. Knot tables are organized by listing prime knots according to their minimal crossing number, the standard census of the subject.

label: Unique Factorization
notes: State the theorem of Schubert: every knot factors as a connected sum of prime knots, and this factorization is unique up to order. The proof rests on additivity of the genus, which forbids infinite descent. Knots thus form a free commutative monoid on the primes, exactly mirroring the integers under multiplication.

label: Recap
notes: Close the lecture. Connected sum makes knots into a commutative monoid with the unknot as identity and no inverses, prime knots are the indecomposable pieces, and Schubert's theorem gives unique factorization into primes. With this structural picture, the next lecture builds concrete numerical invariants of individual knots.
